feedback: If a jump of 20 is drawn the same length as a jump of 7, compare the two side by side against a ruler or scaled line so magnitude maps to length.
If the arrow is read as its endpoint ('+20' read as '58'), ask: does this arrow show the number 58, or does it show 'add 20'? What is the difference?
If subtraction is drawn going right, re-establish that subtraction moves left (gets smaller) and that a jump STARTS from the current number.
If the first addition jump is anchored at 0 instead of at 38, point out that the jump starts from the number you already have.
activities.intendedInsight: Distance on the line equals the amount: a jump represents 'add/subtract this much', not the point it lands on. Addition moves forward and subtraction moves backward, and partitioning a jump mirrors the mental place-value strategy.
learnerActions: Start at 38 on a number line and add a forward jump of 20, then a forward jump of 7, landing on 58 then 65 (showing 38 + 27 = 65).
Notice and state that the +20 jump is drawn visibly longer than the +7 jump because the LENGTH of the jump is the amount.
Build 52 − 24 yourself using backward (leftward) jumps, e.g. −20 then −4, or −22 then −2 bridging 30, landing on 28.
Label each jump with its size and label the start and end points.
Both interpret a diagram you are given and construct one for a new calculation.
activities.title: Build the jump: make each arrow's length equal the amount

feedback: If the first mark is counted as 'one' of the jump, re-run it counting the gaps between marks instead.
If endpoints come out one off, re-step the jump labelling each space as you cross it.
activities.intendedInsight: The amount is the number of intervals jumped, not the number of tick marks counted — this is the classic off-by-one trap.
learnerActions: On a pre-marked, equally spaced number line, label the SPACES (intervals) between the marks rather than the marks themselves.
Physically step out a jump, counting the gaps crossed, not the ticks touched.
Check an endpoint: for a jump of 20 from 38, confirm it lands on 58 and not one mark off.
activities.title: Label the spaces, not the marks

feedback: Reading correctly but drawing flawed lines (unequal spacing, starting from 0, or confusing amount with endpoint) shows partial command — practise producing lines from a blank start.
If spacing in a drawing doesn't match magnitude, compare against a ruler or scaled line.
Note: a hand-drawn or illustrated line is evocative, not exact, so proportional spacing can only be checked roughly; use a ruler or scale to tighten it.
activities.intendedInsight: Reading a diagram and faithfully producing one are different skills; full command means you can do both, reading jumps as amounts and drawing proportional, correctly-directed lines.
learnerActions: Interpret: shown a number line starting at 38 with an arrow landing on 58 labelled '+20' and then an arrow landing on 65 labelled '+7', state what calculation it shows (38 + 27 = 65) and what each jump means.
Explain that 27 has been partitioned into 20 and 7, each a forward jump of that amount.
Translate: on a blank line, draw a number line to show 52 − 24, using backward jumps totalling 24, landing on 28, with start, end, and each jump labelled and spaced proportionally.
Match number-line diagrams to the equations they represent.
activities.title: Interpret a given diagram, then draw your own
